cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that New York's fair-preponderance standard was unconstitutional and that the Due Process Clause requires a State to support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence before permanently terminating parental rights.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: This is the federal constitutional floor that Louisiana codified in La. Ch.C. art. 1035(A) and that the Louisiana Supreme Court cites directly in State in the Interest of C.F. when terminating rights.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that social workers who received and recorded repeated abuse reports but did not remove the child owed him no affirmative substantive-due-process duty of protection, because the harm was inflicted by a private actor and the State had not taken him into custody.
cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

relevance.DEC-01: Sets the constitutional consequence of a screen-out or unfounded closure: a later injury by the parent generally will not support a federal due-process claim against the agency.
relevance.OUT-06: Controls the federal theory of liability when a child dies after the agency knew of the reports but left him at home.
relevance.FAIL-02: Marks the boundary of the substantive-due-process claim: the constitutional violation in removal cases lies in state action taken, not in state inaction.
relevance.FAIL-03: Confirms that failure to meet child-welfare performance expectations does not itself create a constitutional cause of action.
relevance.FAIL-04: Is the leading authority a family will face when a child dies under agency supervision without ever having been taken into state custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review must be a legislative and administrative accountability mechanism rather than a constitutional tort remedy.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the reasonable-efforts requirement of 42 U.S.C. section 671(a)(15) confers no privately enforceable right under section 1983 and creates no implied private cause of action, leaving enforcement to the Secretary's funding-review machinery.
cases.quote: the "reasonable efforts" language does not unambiguously confer an enforceable right upon the Act's beneficiaries

relevance.INP-09: Explains why federal oversight of state child-welfare performance runs through administrative plan review rather than private suit.
relevance.DEC-06: Means a family denied front-end prevention services cannot sue to compel them under Title IV-E; the remedy is state-law and administrative.
relevance.OUT-04: Relevant because Louisiana's extended foster care program is built on federal Title IV-E funding that this case holds is not privately enforceable.
relevance.FAIL-03: Is the controlling answer to whether a state's federal compliance failure can be litigated by the affected children.
relevance.PMC-01: Confirms that CFSR-type federal monitoring, not private litigation, is the designed enforcement route.
relevance.PMC-02: Places financial-audit and funding-cutoff mechanisms at the center of federal accountability for child-welfare dollars.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the role of administrative and citizen oversight bodies where no private right of action exists.
relevance.PMC-06: Frames the structural gap that citizen data analysis is meant to fill when courts are closed to beneficiaries.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that ICWA section 1912(f) does not bar termination where the Indian parent never had custody, and that section 1912(d)'s remedial-services requirement applies only where the termination would precipitate the breakup of an Indian family.
cases.quote: we hold that §1912(d) applies only in cases where an Indian family's "breakup" would be precipitated by the termination of the parent's rights

relevance.INP-11: Governs how a Louisiana court must apply ICWA's heightened standards once an Indian child is identified, and narrows when active-efforts proof is required.

cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that a child may not be seized from the home absent a court order, parental consent, or exigent circumstances, defined as reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; the warrantless entry into the home was not justified, though the removal itself was reasonable on those facts.
cases.quote: there is reasonable cause to believe that the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse if he remains in his home

relevance.INP-03: Addresses a joint caseworker/deputy entry and sets the constitutional limits on law-enforcement-assisted child-protection contacts.
relevance.INP-06: Shows how far an uncorroborated or partially corroborated hotline report will carry a warrantless intervention.
relevance.INP-08: The opinion expressly separates removals from the home from removals at school, the setting in which educator-generated reports are usually investigated.
relevance.INP-12: Supplies the binding Fourth Amendment definition of the exigency that permits protective custody before a court order.
relevance.DEC-02: Holds that a warrantless entry to interview children is not justified by the investigative purpose alone.
relevance.DEC-04: Is the controlling circuit standard for the emergency-removal decision that La. Ch.C. arts. 619-620 authorize by instanter order.
relevance.FAIL-02: Defines the elements a Louisiana family must prove to establish a section 1983 unlawful-removal claim in this circuit.

cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held that the plaintiffs raised a fact question whether the caseworker violated the child's Fourth Amendment rights, but reversed on qualified immunity because those rights were not clearly established, while holding the mother had consented to the investigative home visit and that silence cannot supply consent.
cases.quote: Although they still must obtain the parent's verbal, affirmative consent before conducting an investigative home interview, they need not obtain that consent again when they appear at the parent's doorstep.

relevance.INP-08: Applies the consent rule to the investigative interview of a child, the step that normally follows an educator's report.
relevance.INP-10: Governs the point at which a screened report escalates into an in-home investigative contact requiring consent, warrant, or exigency.
relevance.DEC-02: Is the binding circuit authority on consent for the investigative home visit and interview that Louisiana requires under La. Ch.C. art. 612.
relevance.ACT-01: Establishes that a family's cooperation with voluntary, non-court services must rest on affirmative consent, not acquiescence.
relevance.FAIL-02: Supplies the qualified-immunity framework a Louisiana plaintiff must overcome in a section 1983 investigation or search claim.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court affirmed reversal of a termination judgment, holding that where reunification is the permanent plan the department must make reasonable efforts to help the parent remove the impediments to reunification - here to obtain suitable and affordable housing - before seeking termination under La. Ch.C. art. 1015(5).
cases.quote: the duty to make reasonable efforts to remove the impediments to reunification does not necessarily stop once the children are removed from the parent's custody

relevance.INP-05: The case began when the mother herself told the agency she could no longer care for her children, the paradigm guardian-request intake.
relevance.INP-12: Describes the instanter order and continued-custody hearing sequence and the reasonable-efforts findings the court must make at each stage.
relevance.DEC-04: Confirms that the court must determine at the instanter stage whether reasonable efforts were made to prevent or eliminate the need for removal.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving a poverty-driven family crisis with services rather than an escalating court track.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds the department accountable for actually delivering the assistance a voluntary or agreed service plan promises.
relevance.ACT-02: Requires the court-approved case plan to contain genuine departmental efforts, not merely parental obligations.
relevance.ACT-05: Shows that protective measures short of termination must be exhausted while reunification remains the plan.
relevance.OUT-01: Is the leading Louisiana statement that reunification remains the primary goal and imposes an ongoing departmental duty.
relevance.FAIL-01: The Supreme Court affirmed appellate reversal of the agency-sought termination for failure of proof on reasonable efforts.
relevance.FAIL-03: Ties the state's reasonable-efforts obligation to the federal Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act framework.
relevance.FAIL-05: Makes clear that a parent's inability to afford housing cannot substitute for proof of the statutory ground.
relevance.PMC-01: Demonstrates judicial enforcement of the same reasonable-efforts measures the federal reviews monitor.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of C.F.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that DCFS proved abandonment and case-plan noncompliance by clear and convincing evidence and that the district court manifestly erred in finding termination contrary to the child's best interest; it reversed and terminated the father's rights, freeing the child for adoption.
cases.quote: First, the State must prove by clear and convincing evidence the existence of at least one ground for termination under La. Ch. Code art. 1015.

relevance.DEC-05: States the evidentiary structure the petition must ultimately satisfy once the department moves from dependency to termination.
relevance.OUT-02: Is the current Louisiana Supreme Court statement of the two-prong termination inquiry: a statutory ground by clear and convincing evidence, then best interest.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of A.L.D. and L.S.D.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the court of appeal and reinstated the district court's termination judgment, holding that the court of appeal disregarded the manifest error standard and failed to focus on the children's best interests.
cases.quote: An appellate court reviews a district court's findings as to whether parental rights should be terminated according to the manifest error standard.

relevance.ACT-04: The children were placed with their great-uncle, and the court treated that kinship placement as part of the permanency calculus rather than a substitute for it.
relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the governing standard of appellate review for every Louisiana termination judgment.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of S.M.W.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the court of appeal and reinstated the trial court's termination judgment, holding that the trial court's findings under La. Ch.C. art. 1015(5) were reasonable and not manifestly erroneous and that the court of appeal had failed to focus on the children's best interests.
cases.quote: the primary concern of the courts and the State remains to secure the best interest for the child, including termination of parental rights if justifiable grounds exist and are proven

relevance.OUT-02: States the best-interest orientation that controls the second prong of the Louisiana termination inquiry.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is the leading example of the Supreme Court correcting an appellate reversal that substituted its own view of the evidence for the trial court's.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held the juvenile court exceeded its authority by ordering the department to move a child adjudicated in need of care into a certified foster home, because La. Ch.C. art. 672(A) gives the department sole authority over placement, with judicial control exercised through approval and review of the case plan.
cases.quote: the court was without authority to order the child's movement to a certified foster home

relevance.INP-04: Marks the outer limit of a judge's power to direct agency action in a dependency case.
relevance.DEC-06: Locates judicial leverage in case-plan approval and review rather than in direct command of the agency's service choices.
relevance.ACT-02: Sets out the case-plan filing, objection, approval and periodic-review scheme of La. Ch.C. arts. 673, 677, 688-700.
relevance.ACT-03: Is the controlling Louisiana authority on who chooses the foster placement once custody is assigned to the department.
relevance.OUT-01: Frames the court's supervisory role over the plan that must move the child toward a permanent home.
relevance.OUT-04: Governs the allocation of authority over placement and resources that continues to control a youth's setting as a case approaches or passes the age of majority.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the juvenile court's refusal to find the infant a child in need of care, holding that expert medical evidence of repeated non-accidental trauma established reasonable grounds and that the agency need only prove the petition's allegations by a preponderance.
cases.quote: It is not the OCS's duty to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, by clear and convincing evidence, or to disprove every hypothesis of innocence.

relevance.INP-01: Arose from a verified complaint supported by treating and staff physician reports, the classic mandated medical report.
relevance.INP-02: Confirms that the verified complaint, whatever its source, is tested against the preponderance standard rather than a criminal one.
relevance.INP-03: Illustrates the parallel protective track in a suspected shaken-baby case that would also generate a criminal referral.
relevance.INP-06: Shows how a report of unexplained injury is converted into a judicial finding of reasonable grounds.
relevance.INP-07: The treating physician's affidavit and the agency staff physician's report were the evidentiary core of the case.
relevance.INP-10: Describes the escalation from verified complaint to instanter order to continued-custody hearing.
relevance.INP-12: Is the leading Louisiana Supreme Court decision on the instanter custody order and the continued-custody hearing that follows it.
relevance.DEC-01: Demonstrates that a juvenile court's decision to close the matter and return the child is reviewable and may be reversed.
relevance.DEC-03: Supplies the burden of proof governing the agency's substantiation of abuse in the judicial forum.
relevance.DEC-04: Shows the emergency-removal sequence under La. Ch.C. arts. 619-624 and the proof required to continue custody.
relevance.DEC-05: Is the controlling authority on what the department must show to open and maintain a child-in-need-of-care case.
relevance.ACT-01: The juvenile court had ordered six months of protective supervision in lieu of custody, the court-adjacent service option.
relevance.ACT-03: Holds that placing the child in agency custody was warranted to allow further investigation, case planning and protection.
relevance.ACT-05: Addresses the protective-supervision order the juvenile court entered as an alternative to removal.
relevance.OUT-05: Reverses a dismissal-type disposition that returned the child home despite medical proof of non-accidental injury.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that an alleged father's actual knowledge of the birth and surrender does not substitute for the legal notice the Children's Code requires, so the appellate court erred in treating actual knowledge as sufficient; the mother's act of surrender was dissolved on remand.
cases.quote: the right to notice and an opportunity to be heard must be granted at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner

relevance.OUT-02: Governs the notice due an alleged or adjudicated father before his rights can be extinguished through surrender and adoption.

cases.case_name: Todd v. State Through Department of Social Services, Office of Community Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed judgments against a caseworker and the State for a child's suicide after an abuse investigation, holding the manner of investigation is discretionary and that the mother failed to prove the suicide was reasonably foreseeable or causally linked to the caseworker's conduct.
cases.quote: The manner in which the investigation is conducted is one of discretion, unless the investigation is so incomplete that it could not be found to be thorough.

relevance.INP-01: Sets out La. Ch.C. arts. 611 and 612, the immunity and priority-setting provisions that frame every mandated report.
relevance.INP-02: Explains the good-faith immunity that protects any person who reports, cooperates in the investigation, or participates in the proceedings.
relevance.INP-03: Describes the intake and response-priority scheme that governs referrals from any source, including law enforcement.
relevance.INP-06: Addresses what the agency must do with a report alleging immediate substantial risk of harm.
relevance.INP-07: The investigation followed an allegation of physical abuse and turned on what medical and psychological history the caseworker could be expected to uncover.
relevance.INP-10: Is the controlling Louisiana statement of the standard of care for the investigative stage of a CPS case.
relevance.DEC-01: Defines how far a court will second-guess an agency decision to close or limit an investigation.
relevance.DEC-02: Supplies the discretion-versus-thoroughness test for an accepted investigation, including timeliness of the face-to-face contact.
relevance.OUT-06: Is the leading Louisiana decision on agency liability where a child dies during or shortly after agency involvement.
relevance.FAIL-04: Establishes that foreseeability and causation, not hindsight, control a wrongful-death claim against a caseworker.
relevance.PMC-04: Shows why systemic fatality review, rather than tort litigation, is the realistic accountability mechanism in Louisiana.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that a Children's Code guardianship may be modified or terminated only under La. Ch.C. art. 724, which requires the mover to prove by clear and convincing evidence a substantial and material change in the circumstances of the guardian or the child, not under the Civil Code best-interest custody standard.
cases.quote: we hold that the proper standard for determining whether an order of guardianship should be modified or terminated is statutorily prescribed by Article 724 of the Children's Code

relevance.OUT-03: Is the controlling Louisiana authority on the durability of guardianship permanency and what a parent must prove to undo it.

cases.case_name: New Orleans Bulldog Society v. Louisiana Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that a private nonprofit performing a governmental function under a cooperative endeavor agreement and paid with public money is an instrumentality of the municipality subject to the Public Records Law, and that contractual reporting requirements cannot substitute for public-records access.
cases.quote: the requirement for access to public records cannot be circumscribed by contract

relevance.INP-09: Means privatized child-welfare contractors performing state functions can be compelled to open their records to oversight.
relevance.FAIL-06: Forecloses the argument that a contract's reporting terms discharge an entity's public-records obligations.
relevance.PMC-02: Supports records-based auditing of nonprofit entities receiving public child-welfare dollars.
relevance.PMC-03: Gives citizen review bodies a legal basis to reach records held by contracted providers.
relevance.PMC-05: Is the leading recent Louisiana decision on who counts as a public body for records purposes.
relevance.PMC-06: Establishes the records access on which independent cross-analysis of contracted state functions depends.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held that recorded pre-trial witness statements in a concluded criminal prosecution are public records not exempted by the Public Records Act and not shielded as attorney work product after final adjudication.
cases.quote: the right of access to public records is a fundamental right guaranteed by La. Const. art. XII § 3

relevance.FAIL-06: States the constitutional presumption of access against which any agency withholding must be measured.
relevance.PMC-03: Supplies the interpretive rule that doubts about access are resolved in favor of the public.
relevance.PMC-05: Is the foundational Louisiana authority for a transparency request and for challenging claimed exemptions.
relevance.PMC-06: Anchors the public data pipeline on which independent analysis of state records depends.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal affirmed the denial of the mother's motion to modify a disposition placing the child with her adult half-brother and affirmed the appointment of the half-brother as guardian, finding no manifest error in the conclusion that guardianship was the most appropriate permanent plan.
cases.quote: The trial court may modify a judgment of disposition on its own motion or on the motion of the district attorney, the department, the child or his/her parents.

relevance.INP-04: Shows the juvenile court's continuing authority to revisit disposition on its own motion or on any party's motion.
relevance.ACT-02: Places the burden of justifying modification of a court-ordered disposition on the party seeking the change.
relevance.ACT-04: Approves placement with an adult sibling and discusses La. Ch.C. art. 627(B)'s relative-placement preference.
relevance.OUT-03: Is a worked example of kinship guardianship selected as the permanent plan over a parent's objection.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Third Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal dismissed the mother's appeal as untimely, holding that La. Ch.C. art. 332's fifteen-day delay, not the Code of Civil Procedure delays for custody appeals, governs appeals from judgments in child in need of care proceedings, and that appeal delays are jurisdictional and cannot be extended.
cases.quote: La.Code Civ.P. art. 3492, which sets forth the delay for an appeal from a judgment awarding custody, is inapplicable in child in need of care proceedings

relevance.OUT-05: Shows that a judgment ending the dependency case and awarding custody to a non-parent is still a Children's Code judgment with the shortened appeal delay.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is the trap that most often forecloses appellate correction of an adverse juvenile-court ruling in Louisiana.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, First Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal held that an indigent mother appealing the termination of her parental rights had been deprived of the assistance of counsel when appointed counsel was allowed to withdraw without a replacement, and ordered new counsel appointed to brief her appeal as an active advocate.
cases.quote: Constitutional due process mandates the appointment of counsel to represent indigent parents in proceedings where the state seeks to terminate parental rights to a minor child.

relevance.OUT-05: Establishes that an indigent parent cannot be left to litigate the end of her case pro se after counsel withdraws.
relevance.FAIL-01: Is the Louisiana authority for setting a termination appeal back on track where the parent was effectively unrepresented.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
cases.holding: Applying the judicially created existing-Indian-family exception, the court of appeal held ICWA inapplicable to the adoption of a child who had never lived in an Indian environment, reversed the portion of the judgment allowing the Indian mother to withdraw her consent, and left custody with the non-Indian adoptive couple.
cases.quote: In sum, we find that the adoption of A.S.L. will not cause the breakup of an existing Indian family or removal of a child from an Indian environment.

relevance.INP-11: Is the only published Louisiana appellate decision retrieved applying ICWA, and it must be read against 25 C.F.R. 23.103(c), which rejects the existing-Indian-family exception it applies.
relevance.FAIL-05: Shows the doctrinal route by which Indian children were historically placed outside their tribes notwithstanding ICWA's stated purpose.

cases.case_name: Department of Children & Family Services in the Matter of Fregener Davis Henderson
cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal affirmed the administrative law judge's decision upholding DCFS's valid finding of neglect by dependency and the placement of the appellant's name on the State Central Registry, holding DCFS carried its burden by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: It has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that its determination of a valid finding of child neglect by dependency should be upheld.

relevance.INP-07: The valid finding rested on physician and therapist statements about the child's unmet medical and developmental needs.
relevance.INP-09: Describes how registry findings feed the background-check systems used by education and child-care licensing.
relevance.INP-10: Traces the path from Tier 2 investigation to a valid determination and registry listing.
relevance.DEC-02: Shows what a documented, thorough DCFS investigation looks like when tested on administrative review.
relevance.DEC-03: Is the operative Louisiana authority on the La. Ch.C. art. 616.1.1 administrative appeal of a justified or valid substantiation and the proof DCFS must offer.
relevance.FAIL-01: Sets out the grounds on which a court may reverse or modify an agency determination that prejudices substantial rights.
relevance.FAIL-06: Explains what the State Central Registry is and who may access it, the precondition for any transparency claim about it.
relevance.PMC-05: Documents the registry as a state database whose accuracy and disclosure rules are subject to judicial review.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of G.H.
cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal denied the motion to dismiss and affirmed the juvenile court's denial of former foster parents' third motion to intervene, holding intervention by an interested person under La. Ch.C. art. 697 is discretionary and was properly refused where it would slow the permanency plan.
cases.quote: The trial court is vested with the discretion to allow an intervention as an "interested person."

relevance.ACT-03: Is the Louisiana authority on foster parents' limited standing to contest a change of foster placement, and on DCFS's authority to decide where a child in its custody is placed.
relevance.ACT-04: Arose from a change of placement from the foster parents to a relative-side caregiver and shows how competing intervention claims are resolved.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal affirmed the change of the child's permanent plan to adoption after three adjudications, nine placements and nearly five years in foster care, holding the court must select the plan most appropriate and in the child's best interest and that the department had exceeded reasonable efforts at reunification.
cases.quote: The court is required to determine the permanent plan for the child that is most appropriate and in the best interest of the child.

relevance.INP-05: The parents repeatedly sought and received services over five years without achieving stability, the outer limit of voluntary engagement.
relevance.ACT-02: Illustrates how sustained failure to make measurable progress on a court-approved case plan drives the permanency decision.
relevance.OUT-01: Marks the point at which reunification ceases to be the appropriate permanent plan under Louisiana law.
relevance.OUT-03: Compares guardianship with adoption as competing permanency options and explains why adoption was selected.

cases.court: Court of Appeal of Louisiana, Second Circuit
cases.holding: The court of appeal affirmed termination of a schizophrenic mother's parental rights, holding that mental illness alone cannot justify termination but that clear and convincing evidence showed her illness rendered her unable to exercise parental responsibilities without exposing the child to substantial risk, with no reasonable expectation of near-term improvement.
cases.quote: Mental illness or disability alone is insufficient grounds to warrant termination of parental rights.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the Louisiana rule for terminations grounded in La. Ch.C. art. 1015(5) and art. 1036(D)(1) mental-illness proof.
relevance.FAIL-05: Is the authority a parent with a psychiatric disability will invoke against a termination resting on diagnosis rather than demonstrated parenting risk.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty.
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause does not require appointment of counsel for an indigent parent in every parental-rights termination proceeding; the trial court must decide the question case by case under the Mathews v. Eldridge factors, and on this record the refusal to appoint counsel was not a denial of due process.
cases.quote: neither can we say that the Constitution requires the appointment of counsel in every parental termination proceeding

relevance.OUT-05: It is the federal source of the right-to-counsel inquiry that State ex rel. D.A.G. applies when an indigent parent is left unrepresented as her case ends.
relevance.FAIL-01: It supplies the standard an appellate court uses to decide whether the absence of appointed counsel is the procedural error that requires the termination judgment to be set aside.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court upheld the Indian Child Welfare Act against Article I and anticommandeering challenges and vacated the equal-protection and nondelegation rulings for want of standing, leaving ICWA and its placement preferences fully in force in state child-welfare proceedings.
cases.quote: the bottom line is that we reject all of petitioners' challenges to the statute, some on the merits and others for lack of standing

relevance.INP-11: This is the current Supreme Court decision settling ICWA's constitutional footing, so a Louisiana court identifying an Indian child must apply the Act and its placement preferences without regard to the constitutional objections rejected here.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that domicile under ICWA section 1911(a) is a matter of uniform federal law, that twins born off-reservation to reservation-domiciled parents were domiciled on the reservation, and that the tribal court therefore had exclusive jurisdiction, so the state adoption decree was vacated.
cases.quote: We therefore think it beyond dispute that Congress intended a uniform federal law of domicile for the ICWA

relevance.INP-11: It establishes the federal domicile rule and exclusive tribal jurisdiction that a Louisiana court must apply at the moment an Indian child is identified, and it cannot be displaced by state-law notions of abandonment or residence.
relevance.FAIL-05: It is the authority that most directly undercuts the existing-Indian-family exception applied in Hampton v. J.A.L., because it refuses to let individual choices defeat the tribe's interest in its children.

cases.case_name: Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that section 1983 is presumptively available to enforce individual rights unambiguously conferred by Spending Clause legislation unless the statute's own remedial scheme forecloses it, and that the FNHRA provisions at issue create such enforceable rights.
cases.quote: In that respect, our precedent sets a demanding bar: Statutory provisions must unambiguously confer individual federal rights

relevance.FAIL-03: It is the modern framework that must be applied before concluding, on the authority of Suter v. Artist M., that a federal child-welfare requirement is unenforceable by the children it benefits.
relevance.INP-09: It confirms that federal oversight of a spending-program state agency runs through administrative machinery unless the statute unambiguously confers an individual right.
relevance.PMC-01: It marks the narrow conditions under which a beneficiary could litigate rather than rely on CFSR-type federal monitoring.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that FERPA's nondisclosure provisions confer no individual rights enforceable under section 1983, and that nothing less than an unambiguously conferred right will support a section 1983 action to enforce a federal spending statute.
cases.quote: We now reject the notion that our cases permit anything short of an unambiguously conferred right to support a cause of action brought under § 1983

relevance.FAIL-03: It states the rights-creating test that governs whether a state's failure to meet a federal child-welfare standard can be litigated at all by the affected children.
relevance.INP-09: It explains why statutes with an aggregate, funding-directed focus are enforced by federal administrative review rather than by the individuals they benefit.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the court of appeal and reinstated the termination of a mother's parental rights, holding that the State proved a ground under La. Ch.C. art. 1015(5) by clear and convincing evidence and that leaving the children indefinitely in foster care was not in their best interests.
cases.quote: In balancing these interests, the courts of this state have consistently found the interest of the child to be paramount over that of the parent

relevance.OUT-02: It is the Louisiana Supreme Court's leading statement of the two competing interests in an involuntary termination and of the child's paramount interest in permanency, and it is the case State in the Interest of C.F. quotes.
relevance.OUT-01: It holds that permanent placement under La. Ch.C. art. 603 does not include leaving children indefinitely in foster care, which fixes the point at which reunification must give way.

cases.case_name: State in the Interest of S.M.
cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the approval of reunification as the permanency plan, holding that the record contained no evidence of a reasonable expectation of the mother's reformation in the foreseeable future and that the juvenile court abused its discretion; it remanded for an expedited hearing on a new plan.
cases.quote: More than simply protecting parental rights, our judicial system is required to protect the children's rights to thrive and survive

relevance.OUT-01: It is the Louisiana Supreme Court decision holding that reunification may not be approved as the permanent plan without record evidence of the parent's actual reformation, and it is the authority State ex rel. P.B. relies on for the child's right to a stable permanent home.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court held La. R.S. 9:422.8 unconstitutional insofar as it allowed a mother's private surrender to terminate the rights of an unwed father with a protected interest without prior notice and an opportunity to be heard before a neutral decision maker, dismissed the adoption, and placed the child with her natural parents.
cases.quote: It is evident that the statutory method of terminating the natural parent's interest in his child falls short of due process requirements in several respects

relevance.OUT-02: It is the foundational Louisiana authority on the notice and hearing a father is owed before surrender and adoption extinguish his rights, and it is the source of the due-process rule In re A.J.F. later quotes.
relevance.OUT-05: It shows a Louisiana court dismissing an adoption outright once the statutory route to terminating the father's rights was found constitutionally defective.

cases.court: Supreme Court of Louisiana
cases.holding: The Louisiana Supreme Court reversed the lower courts and held that access to public records is a fundamental constitutional right that must be construed liberally, ordering the clerk to allow reproduction of the records by any safe means, free of charge, and assessing attorney's fees.
cases.quote: Whenever there is doubt as to whether the public has the right of access to certain records, the doubt must be resolved in favor of the public's right to see

relevance.PMC-05: It is the foundational Louisiana Public Records Law decision on which Landis v. Moreau rests, and it is the first authority to cite in any transparency demand to a Louisiana child-welfare agency.
relevance.FAIL-06: It places the burden on the withholding agency and resolves every doubt against nondisclosure, which is the rule an agency refusing child-welfare records must overcome.
relevance.PMC-03: It gives a citizen review body the interpretive rule that access may be denied only where a law specifically and unequivocally so provides.
relevance.PMC-06: It establishes that reproduction, not merely inspection, is part of the constitutional right, which is what makes bulk public-records analysis of state data lawful.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
cases.holding: The Fifth Circuit held the caseworker's entry pursuant to a state removal order objectively reasonable and granted the supervisor immunity, but affirmed the denial of qualified immunity to the caseworker for seizing two siblings where, on the plaintiffs' version of the facts, no imminent danger existed.
cases.quote: Gates was not required to give social workers fair notice that imminent danger must exist before a child may be removed without a warrant or court order

relevance.ACT-06: The case arose from a medical-neglect investigation in which the State took custody of a child with Hodgkin's disease so that treatment her parents had refused could be given, the paradigm court-authorized emergency medical care.
relevance.DEC-04: It adapts the Gates exigency factors to a child-endangerment rather than an abuse investigation, listing the severity, duration, frequency and imminence of the danger and the availability of less extreme solutions.
relevance.FAIL-02: It holds that Roe and Wooley had already clearly established the imminent-danger requirement, so a caseworker who removes a child without it is not immune.
relevance.INP-07: The investigation was opened on reports from the child's treating physicians about refused cancer treatment, the medical-disclosure pathway into the system.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that a child's admission to a state mental hospital, whether sought by parents or by the State as guardian of a ward, requires an independent inquiry by a neutral factfinder into whether statutory admission standards are met, plus periodic review, but not a formal adversarial hearing.
cases.quote: Thus, a staff physician will suffice, so long as he or she is free to evaluate independently the child's mental and emotional condition and need for treatment

relevance.ACT-06: It is the controlling federal standard for authorizing immediate psychological or psychiatric care for a child, and it fixes the minimum process due before that care may begin.
relevance.ACT-03: It addresses children who are wards of the State and holds that the agency's decision to place a child in an institution is subject to the same independent medical review as a parent's.

notes: Every case in this brief was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace and curly quotes normalized), taken from the majority or per curiam opinion, and each is 30 words or fewer.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the LA node files are keyword-matched noise - judicial-discipline matters (In re Judge Colbert, In re Judge Medley, In re Foret), bar-admission matters, and In re Henry L. Klein. None is a child-welfare decision and none was retained.

ICWA is the weakest point in Louisiana's case-law layer. The only published Louisiana appellate ICWA decision retrieved, Hampton v. J.A.L. (La. App. 2d Cir. 1995), applies the judicially created 'existing Indian family' exception. That doctrine is expressly rejected by the 2016 BIA regulations at 25 C.F.R. 23.103(c). It is included for INP-11 because it is the only Louisiana authority found, but it should be cited only as history; practitioners must apply 25 U.S.C. 1911-1915 and the current federal regulations. No Louisiana decision applying active efforts, the qualified expert witness requirement, the placement preferences, or transfer to tribal court was located.

No Louisiana appellate authority was found on extended foster care or continuing jurisdiction past 18 (La. R.S. 46:288.2-288.3, Chafee/FCSIAA). OUT-04 therefore rests on State ex rel. L.C.B. (who controls placement and resources for a child committed to DCFS) and on the federal baseline of Suter v. Artist M. (Title IV-E requirements are not privately enforceable). Searches of both the Supreme Court of Louisiana and the Louisiana Court of Appeal for 'extended foster care', 'independent living', 'Chafee' and 'aging out' returned nothing on point.

No Louisiana authority was found on differential response / alternative response as a distinct track (DEC-06). The cases mapped there are the closest analogues actually retrieved: A.T. (a parent's own request for help met with an instanter removal instead of services), L.C.B. (judicial leverage over the non-court case plan), and Suter (no private enforcement of the federal prevention framework).

Louisiana reporter-immunity case law is thin. Davisson v. O'Brien affirms dismissal of a damages suit against a reporting social worker under La. Ch.C. arts. 609 and 611 and reproduces art. 611 in full, but the panel states no free-standing rule of its own; its quoted sentence is the court's statement of its de novo disposition. Todd v. State supplies the operative caseworker-conduct standard and also sets out arts. 611 and 612. Searches for a published decision squarely construing the good-faith / reckless-disregard limits of art. 611 in a child-abuse-report case returned only Davisson, Todd, and Mitchell v. Villien (a gunshot-wound reporting case under La. R.S. 14:403.5, not child abuse, and therefore excluded).

Section 1983 removal and caseworker-search law for Louisiana comes from the Fifth Circuit. Gates, Roe and Wernecke all arise from Texas agencies but are binding circuit precedent in Louisiana. CORRECTED IN THIS PASS: the earlier statement that no published Fifth Circuit decision involving a Louisiana removal was located is wrong. Wooley v. City of Baton Rouge, 211 F.3d 913 (5th Cir. 2000), retrieved and read in this session, is a Louisiana child-seizure case (Baton Rouge police), and it is now mapped at INP-03, INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02. Note that Roe and Wernecke both found (or assumed) a constitutional violation yet granted qualified immunity in part; Gates is the case that clearly established the flexible exigency standard going forward, while Wooley and Roe supplied the 'some evidence of imminent danger' floor that Wernecke held was already clearly established in June 2005.

Two clusters carry no reporter citation on CourtListener and are cited in slip form as instructed: In re L.M.M., Jr., No. 2017-CJ-1988 (La. June 27, 2018) (the case is in fact published at 253 So. 3d 762), and Dept. of Children & Family Services in the Matter of Fregener Davis Henderson, No. 54,610-CA (La. Ct. App. 2d Cir. June 29, 2022). The Henderson cluster is marked 'Published' by CourtListener; the docket number was read off the opinion's own caption. No unpublished memorandum decision was used.

The B.D.L. quote reproduces the opinion's own text, which refers to 'La.Code Civ.P. art. 3492'. The custody-appeal delay articles are La. C.C.P. arts. 3942-3943; the reference appears to be a typographical error in the published opinion. It is quoted verbatim because the instruction requires an exact substring. The holding - that Children's Code art. 332's fifteen-day delay governs and that appeal delays are jurisdictional - is unaffected.

Womack is affirmed in part and vacated in part: the court vacated the child-in-need-of-care adjudication as to two of the children for insufficient proof. Its admission of a videotaped child statement without the La. Ch.C. art. 324 court authorization is fact-bound and rests on a trustworthiness finding plus La. C.E. art. 804(B)(6); it should not be read as dispensing with art. 324.

Suter's continuing scope should be checked against 42 U.S.C. 1320a-2 (the so-called Suter fix) before relying on it broadly. That statute was not retrieved in this session and no statement about its effect is made here. Suter is now read together with Gonzaga University v. Doe and Health and Hospital Corp. v. Talevski, both retrieved and read in this session, which supply the controlling modern test for when a Spending Clause statute creates a section 1983-enforceable right.

Nothing was found in Louisiana case law on children missing or absent from foster care, or on state child-fatality review commissions. OUT-06, FAIL-04 and PMC-04 rest on Todd v. State (the leading Louisiana decision on caseworker liability for a death during agency involvement), State in the Interest of K.G. and T.G. (severe non-accidental injury as a termination ground), and DeShaney (the federal ceiling on constitutional claims).

FAIL-05 has no Louisiana decision squarely on race, religion or retaliation in placement or investigation. It is built from T.P. (disability: mental illness alone cannot support termination), Hampton (the historical route around ICWA's tribal protections), and now Holyfield (the federal decision that forecloses that route). A.T. (poverty and lack of housing cannot substitute for proof of a statutory ground) bears on the same point through its FAIL-05 relevance. MEPA/IEPA and Title VI claims are not represented in the retrieved Louisiana case law.

The PMC-family nodes are oversight constructs rather than litigated doctrines. They are mapped to the authorities that actually control the mechanisms they describe: Suter and now Talevski (when, if ever, federal child-welfare standards are privately enforceable), Title Research Corp. v. Rausch, New Orleans Bulldog Society and Landis v. Moreau (the Louisiana Public Records Law and the constitutional right of access, including against privatized contractors), Henderson (judicial review of an agency database determination), and Todd/DeShaney (the limits of fatality-based liability).

Statutory anchors confirmed while reading the LA node files and relied on in selecting search terms: La. Ch.C. art. 603(18) (mandated reporters), art. 609 (duty to report), art. 611 (immunity), art. 612 (investigation and response priorities), art. 601 (Title VI purpose; health, safety and best interest paramount), arts. 619-624 (instanter order, continued-custody hearing within 3 days, state's burden at that hearing), art. 606 (grounds), art. 665 (preponderance at adjudication), arts. 672-677 and 688-700 (placement authority, case plan, review), art. 697 (intervention by interested persons), art. 616.1.1 (State Central Registry administrative appeal), art. 724 (guardianship modification), arts. 1015, 1035, 1036, 1037, 1039 (termination grounds, burden and best interest), art. 1016 (right to counsel), art. 332 (fifteen-day appeal delay), art. 621 and art. 736 (peace-officer custody without a warrant, construed in Wooley), and La. R.S. 46:288.2-288.3 (extended foster care).

Added Wooley v. City of Baton Rouge, 211 F.3d 913 (5th Cir. 2000), for INP-03, INP-12, DEC-04 and FAIL-02: it is the Fifth Circuit's Louisiana child-seizure decision, holding that absent a warrant or probable cause officials must have some evidence of danger before taking a child, and that La. Ch.C. arts. 621 and 736 did not authorize the taking where no imminent threat existed. It closes the hole flagged in the prior pass and corrects the earlier note.

Added Lassiter v. Department of Social Servs. of Durham Cty., 452 U.S. 18 (1981), for OUT-05 and FAIL-01: it is the controlling federal decision on appointed counsel for indigent parents in termination proceedings and supplies the case-by-case due-process test that State ex rel. D.A.G. and La. Ch.C. art. 1016 operate within. It was not mapped at OUT-02 because that node is already at the six-case ceiling and Lassiter's contribution is procedural rather than evidentiary.

Added Haaland v. Brackeen, 599 U.S. 255 (2023), for INP-11: it is the Supreme Court's current ICWA decision, rejecting the Article I and anticommandeering challenges and vacating the equal-protection and nondelegation rulings for lack of standing, so ICWA and its placement preferences remain fully binding on Louisiana courts.

Added Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield, 490 U.S. 30 (1989), for INP-11 and FAIL-05: it supplies ICWA's purposes, the uniform federal law of domicile, and exclusive tribal jurisdiction under 25 U.S.C. 1911(a), and it is the authority that most directly undercuts the existing-Indian-family exception applied in Hampton v. J.A.L. It should be cited with 25 C.F.R. 23.103(c) wherever Hampton appears.

Added Health and Hospital Corporation of Marion Cty. v. Talevski, 599 U.S. 166 (2023), for FAIL-03, INP-09 and PMC-01: it is the modern framework governing when a Spending Clause statute creates a right enforceable under section 1983, and it is the case that must be applied before Suter v. Artist M. is deployed as the last word on federal child-welfare enforcement.

Added Gonzaga University v. Doe, 536 U.S. 273 (2002), for FAIL-03 and INP-09: it states the rights-creating test - nothing short of an unambiguously conferred right will support a section 1983 action - that Talevski applies and that governs whether a state's federal child-welfare compliance failure is litigable by the children it affects.

Added State ex rel. J.M., 837 So. 2d 1247 (La. 2003), for OUT-02 and OUT-01: it is the Louisiana Supreme Court's leading statement of the child's competing interest in permanency and of the standard governing involuntary termination, it is quoted in State in the Interest of C.F., and it holds that permanent placement does not include leaving children indefinitely in foster care.

Added State in the Interest of S.M., 719 So. 2d 445 (La. 1998), for OUT-01: it holds that reunification cannot be approved as the permanent plan without record evidence of the parent's actual reformation, and it is the decision State ex rel. P.B. relies on for the child's right to a stable permanent home. Its best-interest language also bears on OUT-02, but that node is at the six-case ceiling.

Added In re Adoption of B.G.S., 556 So. 2d 545 (La. 1990), for OUT-02 and OUT-05: it is the Louisiana Supreme Court's foundational decision on notice, the opportunity to be heard, and parental rights in the surrender/adoption context, holding La. R.S. 9:422.8 unconstitutional as applied to an unwed father with a protected interest. It is the actual source of the due-process rule the brief previously attributed only to In re A.J.F.

Added Title Research Corp. v. Rausch, 450 So. 2d 933 (La. 1984), for PMC-05, PMC-03, PMC-06 and FAIL-06: it is the foundational Louisiana Public Records Law decision holding that access is a fundamental constitutional right, that the provision is construed liberally, and that any doubt is resolved in favor of the public. Landis v. Moreau cites it as the source of the rule the brief quotes Landis for.

Added Wernecke v. Garcia, 591 F.3d 386 (5th Cir. 2009), for ACT-06, DEC-04, FAIL-02 and INP-07: it is a medical-neglect case in which the State took custody of a child with Hodgkin's disease so refused treatment could be given, it adapts the Gates exigency factors to a child-endangerment investigation, and it holds that Roe and Wooley had already clearly established the imminent-danger requirement.

Added Parham v. J. R., 442 U.S. 584 (1979), for ACT-06 and ACT-03: it is the controlling federal standard for authorizing immediate psychiatric or psychological care for a child, including a child who is a ward of the State, requiring an independent inquiry by a neutral factfinder and periodic review but not a formal adversarial hearing.

Could not verify in this session: Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997). It was named by the verifier as part of the Spending Clause / section 1983 line but was not separately searched or retrieved, so no entry is made for it and nothing in this brief rests on it. The line is represented instead by Gonzaga University v. Doe and Health and Hospital Corp. v. Talevski, both retrieved and read here; Talevski's and Gonzaga's own characterizations of Blessing were not used as a substitute for reading Blessing.

ACT-06 (emergency medical / psychological care) has no on-point Louisiana authority. Searches of the Supreme Court of Louisiana and the Louisiana Court of Appeal for court-ordered or emergency medical treatment of a child in state custody, medical neglect, psychiatric hospitalization of a minor, and refusal of necessary medical treatment returned nothing squarely on the decision point. ACT-06 therefore rests on the federal standard (Parham v. J. R.) and on the Fifth Circuit's Louisiana-binding medical-neglect removal case (Wernecke v. Garcia), as permitted by the instruction to supply the federal standard where no state authority exists.

The node_map was extended in this pass in two ways: by adding the twelve new cases, and by reconciling it with relevance keys already present in the existing case entries (for example State ex rel. L.B. at INP-01, INP-02, INP-03, INP-06, DEC-01, ACT-01 and OUT-05; State ex rel. L.C.B. at INP-04 and OUT-04; State ex rel. K.K. at INP-04; State ex rel. P.B. at INP-05; State ex rel. B.D.L. and State ex rel. D.A.G. at OUT-05). No existing case entry was altered. Every one of the 42 nodes now carries between two and six cases and no case is left unmapped.

OUT-02 is capped at six cases by the coverage rule, so State in the Interest of S.M.W., State ex rel. T.P. and State in the Interest of S.M. are not listed there even though each opinion's relevance entry addresses the termination inquiry; each remains mapped elsewhere (FAIL-01, FAIL-05 and OUT-01 respectively). Readers working on OUT-02 should treat those three as additional Louisiana authority on the best-interest prong and on the manifest-error standard.

CourtListener records the date_filed for the Lassiter cluster (110506) as 1981-08-28, which is the date of the amended report rather than the date the opinion was announced. The cluster value is reproduced here because every field in this brief is taken from the retrieved record rather than from memory; the year, 1981, and the reporter citation, 452 U.S. 18, are unaffected.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. J.A., 752 So. 2d 806 (La. 2000) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 7790323). A leading Louisiana Supreme Court termination decision on the child's competing interest in permanency; it is one of the authorities State ex rel. J.M. relies on for the paramount-interest rule the brief quotes J.M. for, and a practitioner briefing OUT-02 would expect it cited alongside J.M. and C.F.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. C.J.K., 774 So. 2d 107 (La. 2000) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 7797357). Louisiana Supreme Court termination decision quoted in J.M. for the balancing of parental and child interests; belongs with OUT-02 and OUT-01 as part of the line the current brief represents only through J.M.

Missing (for a later pass): State ex rel. G.J.L., 791 So. 2d 80 (La. 2001) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 7802023). The decision J.M. cites first for the proposition that the child's interest is paramount; it is the immediate source of the rule the brief attributes to J.M. and should be cited at OUT-01 and OUT-02.

Missing (for a later pass): State in Interest of L.L.Z. v. M.Y.S., 620 So. 2d 1309 (La. 1993) — verified on CourtListener (cluster 1811264). The earlier Louisiana Supreme Court statement on permanency planning that State in the Interest of S.M. was granted specifically to 'expound upon'; OUT-01 is incomplete without it.

Missing (for a later pass): Blessing v. Freestone, 520 U.S. 329 (1997) — the middle step of the Spending Clause / section 1983 line the brief builds from Suter, Gonzaga and Talevski. The brief's own notes concede it was never retrieved. FAIL-03 and INP-09 rest on a three-case chain with its central link missing, and Talevski expressly works through the Blessing factors.

Missing (for a later pass): M.L.B. v. S.L.J., 519 U.S. 102 (1996) — the Supreme Court's holding that a State may not condition appeal of a parental-rights termination decree on the parent's ability to pay record-preparation fees. It is the natural federal companion to Lassiter and State ex rel. D.A.G. at OUT-05 and FAIL-01, where the brief currently has only Lassiter's case-by-case counsel test and B.D.L.'s jurisdictional appeal-delay trap.

Missing (for a later pass): Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) — the foundational unwed-father due-process decision that In re Adoption of B.G.S. expressly builds on (the B.G.S. majority reasons directly from Stanley in the passage the brief quotes). OUT-02 cites B.G.S. and A.J.F. without the federal decision that generates their rule.
